title: The river from the Temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12)
hookLine: a river deepens and heals the salt sea; everything lives where it goes

lines: A RIVER TOO DEEP TO CROSS.
cards: Then water to swim in. Near the end of his book, Ezekiel is shown a vision of the Temple rebuilt, and his guide brings him back to the door of the house. There's water seeping out from under the threshold, flowing east.
A trickle. The guide walks out with a measuring line, measures a distance, and leads Ezekiel through: the water is to his ankles. Another measure: to his knees.
Another: to his loins. Another, and it's a river he can't cross, waters to swim in.

teach.b: Water that seeps out under a door usually spreads out and soaks away. This water does the opposite.
With no stream feeding it that the text mentions, it keeps getting deeper. Then the guide asks Ezekiel a question: son of man, hast thou seen this?
He's brought back along the bank, and now he sees very many trees on both sides. The river flows down into the desert and into the sea, and the waters are healed.

teach.h: EVERY THING SHALL LIVE WHITHER THE RIVER COMETH.
teach.b: Here's the line the whole chapter turns on, in the King James words: "every thing shall live whither the river cometh." Fishermen will stand on the shore and spread their nets, and the fish will be many.
The trees along the banks will bear fruit every month, and their leaves won't wither.

teach.h: FRUIT FOR MEAT, LEAF FOR MEDICINE.
teach.b: And the last detail: "the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine." Food and healing, from water that started under a door.

Ezekiel's book began with exiles sitting by a foreign river, the Chebar, far from the Temple. Near its end, a river flows out from the Temple, so deep it can't be crossed, bringing life even to the sea.
Some readers hear it as God's presence flowing out from the house. And notice where it starts: not as a river at all, but as a seep under a door, measured again and again as it goes.

how: Jews read Ezekiel 47 within the book's closing vision of a rebuilt Temple (chapters 40–48), and the Talmud remembers Hananiah ben Hezekiah working through those chapters to reconcile their laws with the Torah's.

o: the river Elisha told Naaman to dip in
the river in Babylon where the exiles sat
the river flowing out from the rebuilt Temple

games.q: the river from the Temple — tap the pairs.

s: the river starts wide and gets thinner as it flows
it starts as water under a door and grows until it can't be crossed.
the trees by the river bear fruit every month
their leaves don't wither, and the leaf is for medicine.
the river makes the sea's waters worse
its waters are healed, and fishermen spread their nets there.

games.q: you're Ezekiel. the water was ankle-deep, then knee-deep, then waist-deep. your guide measures again. what do you find?
o: a river too deep to cross.
the water stays at your waist.
games.why: it becomes waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over, and everything lives where it goes.

practice: Find something in your life that's still at the ankles: a practice you just started, a new friendship, something you're learning, maybe even this daily habit.
Without pushing, picture walking a little farther in, ankles, then knees, and let the breath be the measuring line, one length at a time. If you pray, you can ask that it bring life where it goes.

wordCard.voice: Chebar, the foreign river where Ezekiel's exiles once sat, far from the Temple whose own river later heals the sea. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a river or stream, the word for the river in Ezekiel 47.

carryVoice: Your line: everything lives where it flows. Even a trickle can become a river. See you tomorrow.
